title: Can injuries be attributed to bad luck?
summary: NH rejects the fatalistic view that injuries just happen. Proper form is mandatory, alongside volume, fatigue and within-set technique management. His 'freak' injuries with good form were minor and healed in a day, while his serious, months-long setbacks came from poor form and ignoring fatigue. Blaming bad luck is a way to dodge responsibility.

claims.claim: The two extremes, 'perfect form means you never get injured' and 'injuries are pure luck, form doesn't exist', are straw men; most people sit somewhere in between, as does he.
Proper form is not just important but mandatory if you want to lift for a long time without setbacks or getting hurt.
There is no universal perfect form, but there are universal cues and aspects of form that must be respected.
Volume and fatigue management matter as much as form; perfect form with poorly managed volume eventually exceeds your ability to adapt and leads to injury.
Fatigue management includes technique within a set: stop the set when technique starts degrading to a dangerous point, even if you could grind out more reps.
Form deniers cite outliers, like people deadlifting with a rounded lower back for 10 years or benching with flared elbows without injury, to justify their methods.
Believing injury can strike at random is not freeing; it increases anxiety, whereas feeling in control of your destiny is better.
He has had 'freak' injuries with good form and managed fatigue, but they were never bad; he recovered within a day, so they were minor hurts rather than injuries.
His real injuries, with setbacks lasting months where he couldn't lift or move, all came from poor form, not listening to his body and accumulated fatigue, and were his own fault.
The 'injuries just happen' mentality exists because it absolves people of responsibility.
Many lifters, including small YouTube channels, take form critiques as personal attacks and find excuses (e.g. 'I've lived longer than you') to reject help that would benefit them.
He has interrupted his own training to help someone in the gym about to get hurt, only to be ignored, but will always offer help to people who look like they don't know what they're doing.
Attributing injuries to bad luck is irresponsible and a weak mentality; you control how your body moves and therefore your injury rate.
Compared with three years ago he now has much less injury and pain and better gains because he can train consistently without skipping days and always feels fresh.
Adopt the mindset behind his methods rather than necessarily his exact protocol, which may not work for you.
